title: FINDER and MGTP Automated Constraint & Model Generators Settle Open Quasigroup Existence Problems QG3–QG7
whyItMatters: Automated model generators FINDER and MGTP solved multiple long-open finite-algebra and combinatorial design existence problems (quasigroups QG3–QG7), proving AI search engines could resolve frontier mathematical open questions.
summary: Presented at IJCAI 1993, Masayuki Fujita, John Slaney, and Frank Bennett applied automated finite-model generators and theorem provers (FINDER and MGTP) to open existence problems in idempotent quasigroups and Latin square designs (QG3 through QG7). By translating algebraic identities into constraint-satisfaction and clause-based search problems with automated symmetry breaking, the systems autonomously constructed new quasigroups and proved non-existence for several previously open orders (such as QG5(12) and QG6(9)), earning landmark status in automated reasoning three years before EQP solved the Robbins Conjecture.
technicalHighlights: Autonomously resolved multiple open orders of finite quasigroup existence problems (QG3–QG7) in combinatorial design theory.
Combined clause-based automated theorem proving (MGTP) with constraint-driven finite model generation (FINDER).
Established finite model generation as a core pillar of AI-assisted mathematical discovery alongside equational proving and SAT.
caveats: Solved specific finite orders of open quasigroup problems rather than general infinite-family classification theorems.
institutions: ICOT (Institute for New Generation Computer Technology)

scoreRationale.foundational: Multiple genuine open finite-algebra and design-theory problems resolved directly by automated AI model generators.
scoreRationale.ripple: Pioneered finite-model-finding and symmetry-breaking techniques foundational to modern SAT/SMT mathematical proving.
scoreRationale.verification: Peer-reviewed in IJCAI 1993 with explicitly checkable finite algebraic models and exhaustive non-existence proofs.
scoreRationale.velocity: Resolved open algebraic orders in hours to days of automated search.
